encounters.cc: Progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and leg swelling after running out of furosemide one week ago

lines: Progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and leg swelling after running out of furosemide one week ago

The patient is a 68-year-old male with known ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction and prior evaluation in January 2020 for dyspnea and weight gain, now presenting with progressive symptoms.
Over the past 10 days, he has become increasingly dyspneic while climbing stairs and now wakes up at night gasping for air.
He also reports feeling bloated, with reduced appetite and weight gain despite minimal food intake.
He ran out of furosemide one week ago and has not refilled it.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF 25-30%)
- History of anterior wall myocardial infarction
- History of lateral wall myocardial infarction
His past medical history includes chronic systolic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30%), hypertension, and a remote history of anterior wall myocardial infarction.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (anterior wall)
His current medications include carvedilol, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, and furosemide.
- Warfarin 5 mg PO daily (titrate to INR 2.0-3.0)
- Mother: Hypertension and chronic kidney disease
Smoking: Former smoker, 30 pack-years, quit 5 years ago.
His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, and respiratory rate is 22/min.
On examination, the patient appears fatigued and mildly tachypneic.
Jugular venous distension is noted 8 cm above the sternal angle at 45°.
Cardiac auscultation reveals a displaced apical impulse and an S3 gallop.
Lung examination shows bilateral basilar crackles.
There is 3+ pitting edema in both lower extremities to the mid-shin and ascites is suspected based on shifting dullness.
His serum sodium remains stable, but his potassium level drops to 3.2 mEq/L.
Bedside ultrasound shows a dilated inferior vena cava with minimal collapse during inspiration.
A chest X-ray reveals pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions.
The patient is admitted and receives intravenous furosemide.
Within 6 hours, his urine output increases substantially, his dyspnea improves, and his oxygen requirements decrease.
Repeat physical exam shows improved JVP and clearer lungs.
The medical team discusses the pharmacologic mechanism of loop diuretics and their effect on renal electrolyte handling.

encounters.cc: Severe chest pressure in the center of the chest radiating to the left arm and jaw with shortness of breath and diaphoresis

lines: Severe chest pressure in the center of the chest radiating to the left arm and jaw with shortness of breath and diaphoresis
This patient with HFrEF and prior MI presents with chest pain after HF exacerbations.
The pain is described as a heavy pressure in the center of his chest, radiating to his left arm and jaw.
He also reports shortness of breath and diaphoresis.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF 25-30%)
- History of anterior wall myocardial infarction
- History of lateral wall myocardial infarction
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (anterior wall)
His medications include atorvastatin and lisinopril.
- Warfarin 5 mg PO daily (titrate to INR 2.0-3.0)
- Mother: Hypertension and chronic kidney disease
Smoking: Former smoker, 30 pack-years, quit 5 years ago.
On examination, his blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air.
Physical examination reveals jugular venous distension, bilateral crackles halfway up both lung fields, and a third heart sound (S3).
An echocardiogram reveals severe hypokinesis of the left ventricular inferior wall.
An electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.
The patient is started on oxygen, aspirin, and nitroglycerin.
Despite these measures, his blood pressure remains low.
